questions.prompt: Which context tells you the name of the branch or tag that triggered the run?
questions.explain: github.ref_name is the short name; github.ref is the full ref, such as refs/heads/main.

questions.prompt: An if condition never fires, and you suspect a typo in a context name. What does GitHub do with an unknown context?
choices: Usually evaluates it to an empty string, so the condition is simply false
Skips the job with a warning
questions.explain: It quietly becomes empty, which is why printing the expression in a run step is the fastest way to see what it held.

questions.prompt: Which function turns a JSON string into data you can index?
questions.explain: fromJSON parses a string into real data, which is how dynamic matrices are built later.

questions.prompt: A step has if: github.event_name == 'push'. An earlier step failed. Does it run?
choices: Yes, the condition is about the event only
No, because every if carries an invisible success() unless you write a status function
Yes, if the job has continue-on-error
Only if it is the last step
questions.explain: The real condition is success() && github.event_name == 'push'.

questions.prompt: You want a step to run even when an earlier one failed, but not when the run is cancelled. What does GitHub recommend?
questions.explain: always() also runs during cancellation and can hold a run open; !cancelled() expresses the intent precisely.

questions.prompt: A step fails with continue-on-error: true. What are its outcome and conclusion?
questions.explain: outcome is before continue-on-error and conclusion after, so the job carries on while the failure stays visible.

questions.prompt: A job that another job needs is skipped. What happens to the dependent job?
choices: It is skipped too, unless its if says otherwise
questions.explain: A failed or skipped dependency skips the jobs that need it, and the skip travels down the chain.

questions.prompt: Where does a non-sensitive setting that differs between environments belong?
questions.explain: Configuration variables exist at organisation, repository, or environment level, and are read with vars.NAME.

questions.prompt: Why should a password never be a variable?
choices: Variables render unmasked in build output
Variables cannot be read in run steps
questions.explain: GitHub's own warning: variables are not masked. Sensitive values belong in secrets.

questions.prompt: Which statement about secret redaction in logs is true?
choices: Every appearance of a secret is always masked
Redaction is not guaranteed, especially if the value is transformed, and covers only the current job
Redaction works across all jobs in the run
Redaction happens only for organisation secrets
questions.explain: Transformations such as base64 can defeat it, and the runner only knows secrets used in the current job.

questions.prompt: How does a step publish a small value for later jobs?
choices: echo name=value >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT", with an id on the step
questions.explain: The step needs an id, writes name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the job re-exports it under outputs.

questions.prompt: How does a dependent job read that value?
questions.explain: The steps context is per job. Across jobs you read needs.<job>.outputs.<name>.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an artifact and a cache?
choices: Nothing, they are two names for the same store
An artifact is output you meant to keep and share; a cache exists to make a later run faster and may vanish
questions.explain: Treating a cache as storage is a common mistake: it is an optimisation and can disappear at any time.

questions.prompt: What does appending Markdown to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY do?
choices: Adds a comment to the pull request
Puts the content on the run's summary page
Creates an annotation on a line of code
Writes to the job log only
questions.explain: Summaries surface results without making anyone read the log; annotations are the ::error file=...:: form instead.
